thread.title: Apple ( AAPL ) announced that it expects to pay $38B in taxe

author: George Kesarios
title: Apple ( AAPL ) announced that it expects to pay $38B in taxe
text:
Apple ( AAPL ) announced that it expects to pay $38B in taxes on the money is has overseas, as part of the changes to the U.S. tax code. This also means that AAPL is expected to repatriate the entire $250B it has in its foreign subsidiaries.
Moving that much money should cause ripple effects in the markets, right? I mean $250B is enough to move the FX market, the bond market and even U.S interest rates, depending on what APPL does. 
But before we answer this questions, let's see the composition of AAPL's so called "cash hoard."

Apple's FORM 10-K Sep. 30 
To begin with, AAPL states in its 10-K report that the company’s "cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities are generally based in U.S. dollar-denominated holdings." So for starters we know that almost all of AAPL's liquid holdings are dollar based.
And if we look at the composition of the holdings in the table above, the only non-dollar denominated holdings are probably the $7.8B in foreign government securities. Everything else is dollar based.
As far the repatriation issue, another question is where are these holding located, that actually require repatriation.
Well the answer is that these holding are not overseas, but located in NY banks. We know this back from 2013 when the U.S. Senate investigated how AAPL and other U.S. multinationals arranged their tax affairs, so as to not pay the 35% tax that everyone else in the U.S. pays. From the NYT :
Apple’s $102 billion in offshore profits is actually managed by one of its wholly owned subsidiaries in Reno, Nev., according to the Senate report on the company’s tax avoidance. The money is tracked by Apple company bookkeepers in Austin, Tex. What’s more, the funds are held in bank accounts in New York.
Because the $102 billion is technically assigned to two Irish subsidiaries, however, the United States tax code considers the money to be under foreign control, and Apple is legally entitled to avoid paying taxes on it.
So basically, the money already is on U.S. soil and already in dollar denominated instruments. And by repatriation, in reality we mean a transfer of these holding from AAPL's Irish subsidiaries (or others), to AAPL itself.
So because AAPL estimates is will pay $38B in taxes, this probably means it will transfer ownership of the entire $250B in liquid assets it has. The only requirement is a transfer of ownership from one company to another.
What this might mean for the markets 
To begin with, because all of AAPL's assets already are in dollar denominated instruments and not in foreign cash or securities, there will be ZERO effect in the FX market. 
At the margin, AAPL already has exchanged the revenue it receives from foreign sales into dollars a long time ago. In fact, I'm assuming as the money comes in, it is exchanged in dollars on the fly.
So do not expect a sudden upward move in the dollar vs the Euro, because APPL will not be exchanging anything into dollars because everything already has been exchanged.
There also will be no repercussion in the U.S. government securities market. AAPL has about $60B in U.S. government securities. While this is a huge number, it is probably not big enough to move interest rates in the market, even assuming AAPL liquidates its position. So don't expect any interest rate moves on U.S. government securities.
AAPL also has about $152B in corporate securities. While we do not know the breakdown of these securities, I'm assuming that most of them are debt instruments of the highest quality from major U.S. corporations. 
If AAPL were to liquidate these securities for some reason, the answer is that yes, it would cause a ripple in the U.S. corporate bond markets. I'm guessing interest rates would spike. By how much and for how long I cannot tell, however it would probably be noticeable. But like I said, this only if AAPL liquidates this position, something that I doubt will happen. 
Please note this article only examines what might happen in the markets as a result of AAPL's so called "asset repatriation," and not AAPL's:
$10B capital expenditures in data centers across the US $55B spending in domestic suppliers $30B in capital expenditures in the US over the next five years and creation of 20,000 new jobs Increasing the size of its Advanced Manufacturing Fund from $1B to $5B Plan to accelerate its efforts across the US in support of coding education. Obviously all these points will have a positive spin on the U.S. economy, but it is not the subject of this article. As far as the markets are concerned, nothing will happen. 
Bottom line AAPL's so called repatriation is nothing more than a transfer of asset ownership from AAPL's foreign subsidiaries to AAPL itself.
AAPL already has almost all its assets in U.S. dollar denominated instruments, therefore there will be no effect in the FX market (dollar, euro yen or otherwise). 
There might be a noticeable interest rate spike in the U.S. corporate debt markets, however only if AAPL liquidates its $152B in corporate debt holdings, something I doubt will happen.
Also note that the same applies to many other U.S. multinationals. According to Bloomberg as of Nov 17, 2017, the top 10 list of companies with assets overseas (AKA U.S. denominated holdings in NY banks) are:
Company Cash & marketable securities ($B) 
held overseas as per latest filing ($B)
Apple 261.5 264 Microsoft ( MSFT ) 138.5 132.1 Cisco ( CSCO ) 70.5 67.5 Alphabet ( GOOGL )( GOOG ) 107.4 60.5 Oracle ( ORCL ) 66.9 58.3 Johnson & Johnson 41.9 41.3 Amgen 41.4 38.9 Gilead 36.6 30.8 Qualcomm ( QCOM ) 38.6 29.4 General Electric ( GE ) 78.6 27 More or less these companies use similar structures to avoid U.S taxation, and their holdings also are dollar based. So even if all these holdings are transferred to their U.S. subsidiaries, nothing noticeable should happen to U.S. or foreign markets. 
As a final note, Bloomberg estimates that $3.1 trillion in assets are stockpiled "overseas." If all those assets get taxed at 15% similar to AAPL, then that might mean $450B in taxes for the U.S. Treasury Department. That's is a lot of money, and at the very least will be a shot in the arm for the U.S. government.
